_comment: One quad each, and one model per facing. Five models, no rotation.
A one-pixel box has four narrow side faces, and a side face is a full
rectangle while the sheet drawn on the large faces has a torn silhouette.
Anything those faces draw — a slice of the map, a plain parchment edge —
stands out past every tear as a solid rectangular rim.
Collapsing the box to a zero-length axis removes those faces but leaves
the up and down quads on exactly the same plane. The renderer has no way
to order two coplanar faces, and because Bedrock shades a downward face
much darker than an upward one, the fight between them reads as the block
flickering black.
Omitting a face from the `uv` map removes it, so each panel here is a
single quad: nothing coplanar with it, no edges, and the torn outline is
the only silhouette there is. It stays visible from both sides because
`alpha_test` does not cull back faces — that is what the later
`alpha_test_single_sided` method was added to do, and the block
deliberately does not ask for it.
── Why five models instead of one and a rotation ─────────────────────
The wall panels used to be a single model turned by
`minecraft:transformation`, with the selection box set separately per
permutation on the assumption that the transform moved the art but not
the box. In a live world the hitbox came out on the same side whichever
face the map was hung on, which is what a transform being applied to the
box as well would look like.
Rather than work out which half of that assumption was wrong, the
transform is gone: each facing has its quad authored where it belongs, so
the art and the selection box are written in the same coordinate space by
hand and nothing is applied to one and not the other.
Each quad sits a quarter-pixel off the surface it is mounted on, so it
cannot z-fight with the face of the block behind it, and is 15 pixels
rather than 16 so it reads as an object resting on a surface rather than
as the surface itself.
The facing names follow `minecraft:block_face`, which records the face of
the block that was built against — so the support is always on the far
side of the map from the viewer, and `..._north` is the panel you see
when looking north-to-south at a wall to its south.
